subject: Reserved GPU concurrency carveout — proposed failover playbook for StellarTech

Date: Sat, 22 May 2027 16:12:00 -0400
Subject: Reserved GPU concurrency carveout — request and proposed fallback

Hi Naomi,

Thanks again for the demo last week. StellarTech is getting close to signing for a 24/7 reserved GPU pool but we need one carveout clarified before procurement can finish: our inference traffic has very spiky concurrency (short, bursty calls at 200–250 RPS for 30–90s every hour). We can tolerate short tail latency increases but cannot accept preemption that drops in-flight requests.

Specifically we need to understand:
- How reserved concurrency is enforced vs. burst capacity.
- Whether in-flight requests on a reserved tenant can be preempted for higher-tier traffic or autoscaling events.
- A proposed failover playbook (falls back to lower-cost models / different region) and any SLA crediting if failover increases 99th-percentile latency beyond our threshold.

I've attached a CSV with a representative 48-hr traffic sample and a one-page summary of our procurement requirements. Procurement will need explicit contract language for a "concurrency carveout" and a failover credit formula.

Can you route this to the right folks? Time is tight — procurement needs an answer for our July board review.

Thanks,
Rajesh
Head of ML Infrastructure
StellarTech

Subject: Proposed carveout + failover crediting (draft)

Rajesh — following up with a concise proposal we can put into the MSA addendum:

1) Concurrency carveout definition
   - Reserved tenant is allocated N reserved concurrent GPU slots (documented as "Guaranteed Concurrency").
   - Bursting above N is permitted up to a short-duration pool-level burst capacity if available, but burst capacity is best-effort and not guaranteed.

2) In-flight request preemption
   - Redwood will not preempt or cancel in-flight requests originating from a Reserved tenant while the request is executing on reserved capacity. In the rare case of hardware fault or maintenance, Redwood will attempt to drain and resume; if failover occurs, Redwood will document duration and apply credits per section 4.

3) Failover options
   - Automatic model-variant fallback (quantized / lower-capacity variant) for degraded capacity (recommended).
   - Regional failover to a matched Reserved pool (subject to data residency controls).
   - Temporary routing to a Dedicated burst pool (best-effort).

4) Credit formula (draft)
   - If 99th-percentile latency for reserved tenant exceeds agreed threshold T for more than X minutes in a 24-hour window due to capacity failover, Redwood will credit Y% of that-day reserved fees proportional to outage duration. Exact T/X/Y to be negotiated; proposal below: T = baseline+150ms, X = 15 minutes, Y = 15%.

I've attached a short playbook PDF with an example escalation path and suggested telemetry for post-incident analysis. Can we run a 72-hour test window against a production-like workload (your CSV looks fine) to validate behavior? If yes, we can produce telemetry and iterate parameters.

Thanks — happy to jump on a quick call.

Ben Carter
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
Attachments: st_playbook_v1.pdf (application/pdf)

Can you commit to a proactive maintenance notice window for Reserved pools (e.g., 48 hours) and an emergency maintenance SLA (e.g., restore within 2 hours or it's considered a failover)?

Subject: Technical playbook: queueing, preemption, and the blackout window

Hi Rajesh — quick technical note on how Reserved pools behave and how we can honor your blackout: 

- Queueing behavior: Reserved concurrency corresponds to N worker slots pinned to your tenant's pool. Incoming requests above N are enqueued with a short-lived queue (configurable max wait time). If queue wait exceeds the configured max, requests are rejected with a clear 429/Retry-After. We can guarantee queuing semantics for Reserved pools with configurable max queue depth and per-tenant queue timeouts.
- Preemption: Redwood's scheduler will not evict in-flight GPU kernels for Reserved slots. Evictions only occur for queued requests during capacity shortages. For emergency rebalancing (data center outage), we treat any failover path as a capacity incident and it triggers the credit formula.
- Maintenance notice & emergency SLA: we can provide 48-hour notice for planned maintenance. For unplanned incidents, our target is 2 hours to restore or failover to a backup regional pool; if that target is missed, it will be treated as a failover for crediting.
- Blackout windows: we can pin a daily 60-minute blackout (02:00–03:00 UTC) during the test window where routing changes are suppressed and no automatic model-variant fallback will be triggered.

Next steps:
1) Ben/legal to produce contract clause with defined T/X/Y and blackout window language.
2) We run a 72-hour test excluding the blackout hour and collect 99th latency, error rate, and NLL/quality metrics.
3) Post-test review for final parameters.

I'll also add a short checklist for the CS runbook (failover contacts, artifacts to collect, and postmortem template).

Laura Bennett
Product Manager, Redwood Inference
